finding.source: request.json["amount"] at bank.py:10 and request.json["to"] at bank.py:9, with no sign check.
finding.sink: BAL[to] += amount at bank.py:14 and BAL[g.user] -= amount at bank.py:13.

trace.note: to = victim taken from request body
BAL[attacker] < -100 is False for a non-negative balance, so abort(400) is skipped

finding.guards_checked: Only check is bank.py:11 which passes for negative amounts. No amount > 0 check in /transfer (contrast bank.py:21 in /withdraw). No recipient existence or ownership check.

verdict.guard_found: Only bank.py:11 (`BAL[g.user] < amount` → abort(400)). It rejects only overdrafts and does not reject negative amounts, so a negative amount passes it. No amount > 0 check exists in /transfer (contrast bank.py:21 in /withdraw), and no recipient existence or ownership check. No auth middleware or g.user setter is in the directory (Glob shows only bank.py), so the attacker is any caller who already has g.user set, i.e. an authenticated low-privilege user.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches bank.py: to is read at line 9, amount at line 10, the only check at line 11 passes for amount=-100, and lines 13–14 credit g.user and debit `to` by 100, with no sign or recipient check anywhere in /transfer.

finding.claim: A NaN amount sets the caller's balance to NaN, after which the balance check never aborts, so arbitrary credit can be minted for any recipient.
finding.source: request.json["amount"] at bank.py:20 accepts the non-standard NaN literal via Python json (Flask default).
finding.sink: BAL[to] += amount at bank.py:14 with an unbounded amount, and BAL[g.user] -= amount at bank.py:23.

trace.note: NaN <= 0 is False and BAL[a] < NaN is False, so the request is not rejected
BAL[a] -= NaN sets attacker balance to NaN
NaN < amount is always False, so the transfer check never aborts
BAL[victim] += 1000000 credits victim with money never debited from anyone

finding.guards_checked: bank.py:21 tests amount <= 0 which NaN bypasses. No math.isfinite or numeric type check on amount in either route. No check on the resulting balance.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. bank.py:21 (`amount <= 0`) is the only validation on amount and NaN bypasses it, and it exists only in /withdraw, not /transfer. bank.py:11 (`BAL[g.user] < amount`) is the balance check, which NaN also bypasses. No math.isfinite or numeric type check exists anywhere in bank.py.
verdict.reason: The NaN mechanics hold: Python json accepts NaN, bank.py:21 and bank.py:11 comparisons are False for NaN, and bank.py:23 turns the balance into NaN, after which bank.py:14 mints unbounded credit. But reachability is undecided because `g.user` is read at bank.py:11, 13, 21, and 23 and is never assigned in the only file present (bank.py is the sole file), so there is no authentication to establish who the attacker is or whether the routes work at all; if the real app sets `g.user` for any logged-in user, this would be CONFIRMED.

finding.claim: Check-then-act race between the balance check and the debit lets concurrent requests overdraw an account.
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount at bank.py:13 (transfer) and bank.py:23 (withdraw).

trace.note: Thread A passes BAL[a] < amount check
Thread B passes the same check before A debits
Thread B debits, balance goes negative

finding.guards_checked: No lock, transaction, or atomic update around check and debit. Flask dev server is threaded by default, so reachable in that configuration. Severity depends on deployment.

verdict.guard_found: none. The check at bank.py:11 (transfer) and bank.py:21 (withdraw) is a plain comparison followed by abort(400), with no lock, transaction, or atomic update around the read at line 11/21 and the debit at line 13/23. No before_request, locking, or threading guard exists in the directory (only bank.py is present).
verdict.reason: The trace matches bank.py:11-13 and 21-23: the balance check and the subtraction are separate, unguarded operations, so concurrent requests from one authenticated user can both pass the check before either debit (the trigger needs a threaded server, which the Flask dev server is by default, and g.user is set by auth code not present here).

finding.claim: Transfer to a nonexistent recipient debits the sender before raising KeyError, destroying the sender's money.
finding.source: request.json["to"] at bank.py:9 not checked for existence.
finding.sink: BAL[to] += amount at bank.py:14 raises KeyError after the debit at bank.py:13 has been applied.

trace.note: to taken from request body, unchecked
KeyError because to is not in BAL; request returns 500 with debit already applied

finding.guards_checked: No existence check on to before debit. No rollback on exception. Impact limited to the caller's own funds.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are the balance test at bank.py:11 and abort(400) at bank.py:12, which run before the debit and do not test whether `to` exists in BAL. Nothing at bank.py:13-14 catches the KeyError, there is no rollback, and no error handler is defined in bank.py.
verdict.reason: The trace holds: `to` comes unchecked from the request at bank.py:9, the debit at bank.py:13 is applied, and `BAL[to] += amount` at bank.py:14 raises KeyError on a missing key (BAL is a plain dict, bank.py:4), so the sender loses funds with a 500 response. The impact is limited to the caller's own balance, so this is a data-integrity bug rather than a cross-user security vulnerability; the attacker is any user whose g.user is set, and g.user's setup is not in the provided files.
